title: Ask how many other ships are in port
subtitle: Your day ashore is set by the total number of passengers landing, not by the ship you chose.

text: Santorini in August is not a place. It is a queue with a view.
sub: Not because the island changed, but because four ships can land their guests into the same six hours and the same cable car.

title: Four variables, all knowable in advance

points.label: Ships in port
points.value: Published schedules, months ahead. Ask before you book, not after you sail.

points.label: Combined capacity
points.value: Three modest ships can land fewer guests than one very large one. Count berths, not hulls.

points.label: Your berth time
points.value: First alongside at dawn is a different island from third at eleven.

points.label: The week of the year
points.value: Deployment thins on the shoulders. Fewer ships are simply scheduled to be there.

title: Three moves that survive high season

items.head: Trade the marquee call
items.body: A quieter island on a busy day is often the better day. The postcard port will keep.

items.head: Take the early hours
items.body: Ashore at seven, back aboard by noon, and let the afternoon crowd have the town.

items.head: Shift the week, not the ship
items.body: The same itinerary a fortnight later frequently has half the company in port.

right.label: Shoulder
items: A table when you want it

text: Crowding is a scheduling fact, not a season-long verdict.
sub: Which means it can be planned around. The work is reading the port schedule and the deployment before the fare is paid.

title: DM me the word CALENDAR
body: I'll send the shoulder-season weeks I'm watching in the Aegean, and which calls I'd avoid in the height of summer.
